t.2.98.1: Then, for those lions among men, surrounded by their bands of friends, the night passed painfully as they went on grieving.
t.2.98.2: When the night had brightly dawned, those brothers, surrounded by their friends, performed the oblations and recited prayers on the Mandākinī, and then approached Rāma.
t.2.98.3: They sat there together in silence, and no one said anything at all; but Bharata, in the midst of his friends, spoke these words to Rāma.
t.2.98.4: My mother has been appeased, and this kingdom has been given to me. I give it to you alone; enjoy the kingdom, free of thorns.
t.2.98.5: Like a dam burst by a mighty rush of water when the rains come, this great breach in the kingdom is hard for anyone other than you to hold back.
t.2.98.6: As a donkey cannot follow the gait of a horse, and as birds cannot follow the flight of Tārkṣya, so I have no power to follow your course, O lord of the earth.
t.2.98.7: Life is always easy for one on whom others depend; but, O Rāma, life is hard for one who depends on others.
t.2.98.8: Just as a tree planted and nurtured by a man grows into a great tree with a sturdy trunk, hard for a short man to climb,
t.2.98.9: If, having come into flower, the tree should bear no fruit to show, then he for whose sake it was nurtured would not enjoy the delight he had hoped for.
t.2.98.11: O great king, let the guilds and the foremost men everywhere behold you, the subduer of foes, established in the kingship, blazing like the sun.
t.2.98.10: This is the simile, O mighty-armed one, and you ought to grasp its meaning: it applies if you, the foremost of men and our master, do not rule us, your servants.
t.2.98.12: O Kākutstha, as you set forth, let the rutting elephants trumpet in your train, and let the women dwelling in the inner apartments rejoice, wholly composed in mind.
t.2.98.13: Having heard the words of Bharata as he entreated Rāma in return, the various people of the city thought, "Well said!"
t.2.98.14: Seeing the illustrious Bharata thus grieving and lamenting, Rāma, perfected in spirit and master of himself, consoled him.
t.2.98.15: A man cannot act as he wishes, for this man is not his own master; fate drags him hither and thither.
t.2.98.16: All accumulations end in dwindling, all heights end in falling, unions end in separation, and life ends in death.
t.2.98.17: Just as ripe fruits have no fear other than that of falling, so a man who has been born has no fear other than that of death.
t.2.98.18: Just as a house, though its pillars be firm, collapses once it has grown old, so too do men sink down when they have fallen under the power of old age and death.
t.2.98.19: The passing days and nights swiftly wear away the lives of all living beings here in this world, just as the sun's rays dry up water in the summer.
t.2.98.21: Death walks along with one, death sits down with one, and having travelled a very long road, death returns together with one.
t.2.98.20: Grieve for yourself; why do you grieve for another? For your own life is wasting away, whether you stand still or move on.
t.2.98.22: Wrinkles have come upon the limbs, and the hairs of the head have turned white; a man worn out by old age, what can he accomplish, by doing what can he show his power?
t.2.98.23: Men rejoice when the sun has risen, and they rejoice when the sun has gone to its setting, yet they do not perceive the wasting away of their own life.
t.2.98.24: People rejoice on seeing the onset of each season arriving here ever new, yet with the turning of the seasons comes the wasting away of the life-breath of living beings.
t.2.98.25: Just as one piece of wood and another might come together on the great ocean, and, having met, might drift apart again when some moment arrives,
t.2.98.26: Even so, wives, sons, kinsmen and riches come together and then run apart, for separation from them is certain.
t.2.98.28: It is just as if someone standing by the road were to say to a caravan passing on its way, "I too shall come along behind you."
t.2.98.27: No living being here acts according to his own will; therefore one who keeps grieving for the departed has no power in that matter.
t.2.98.29: Thus has the road been trodden by those who came before, the certain path of fathers and forefathers. Having entered upon it, why should one grieve, when for it there is no turning aside?
t.2.98.31: That righteous-souled lord of the earth, our father, cleansed of sin by auspicious sacrifices performed in full and rich in sacrificial gifts, has gone to heaven.
t.2.98.30: Since life slips away like a stream that never turns back, one should devote oneself to happiness, for living beings are held to be partakers of happiness.
t.2.98.32: By rightly supporting his dependents, by protecting his subjects, and by taking wealth in accordance with dharma, our father has gone to heaven.
t.2.98.33: Having worshipped with sacrifices of many kinds, having obtained abundant enjoyments, and having attained the highest span of life, the lord of the earth has gone to heaven.
t.2.98.34: For our father, having cast off his worn-out human body, has attained a divine splendour that roams in the world of Brahmā.
t.2.98.36: These griefs of many kinds, and likewise lamentation and weeping, must indeed be shunned in all circumstances by one who is steadfast and wise.
t.2.98.35: But no wise man of this sort ought to grieve for him, no one like you, nor anyone of that kind who is learned and of superior intelligence.
t.2.98.37: So be at ease and do not grieve; go and dwell in that city, for thus you have been appointed by our self-controlled father, O best of speakers.
t.2.98.38: Wherever I too have been appointed by that same man of virtuous deeds, there indeed I shall carry out the command of my noble father.
t.2.98.39: It is not right for me to set aside his command, O subduer of foes. You too should always honor it, for he is indeed our kinsman; he is our father.
t.2.98.40: When Rāma had spoken these meaningful words and fallen silent, the righteous Bharata spoke a wonderful and righteous speech.
t.2.98.41: Who indeed in this world could be such as you are, O subduer of foes? Sorrow would not distress you, nor would joy elate you.
t.2.98.42: You are esteemed by the elders, and you inquire into those doubtful matters; as with one who is dead, so with one who lives, as in what is not, so in what is.
t.2.98.43: He who has gained this understanding, by what could he be tormented? Such a man, even on meeting with misfortune like this, ought not to give way to despair.
t.2.98.44: O Rāghava, you are like the immortals in your nature, great-souled and true to your promises; you are all-knowing, all-seeing, and wise.
t.2.98.45: Sorrow most unbearable ought not to overcome one such as you, endowed with such virtues and knowing well both the origin and the end of things.
t.2.98.46: The sin that my mean-minded mother committed on my account while I was away from home is hateful to me. May you be gracious to me!
t.2.98.47: I am bound by the bond of dharma; therefore I do not here strike down this mother of mine with a fierce rod, though she deserves punishment and is a doer of evil.
t.2.98.48: How could I, born of Daśaratha, whose lineage and deeds were pure, and knowing what dharma is, commit a most unrighteous and despicable deed?
t.2.98.49: Because he is my guru, a performer of sacred rites, aged, a king, now departed, my father, and a deity as well, I would not censure our father in the assembly.
t.2.98.50: For what man who knows dharma, O knower of dharma, would commit such a sinful deed, devoid of both dharma and artha, merely out of a wish to please a woman?
t.2.98.51: There is an ancient saying that at the time of their end, beings become deluded; by acting in this way, the king has made that saying plainly evident in the world.
t.2.98.52: Keeping in view what is right and good, may your honor undo whatever transgression our father committed out of anger, delusion and rashness.
t.2.98.53: For the son who sets right what his father has done amiss, deeming that proper, is regarded in the world as a true offspring; one who acts otherwise is held to be the very opposite.
t.2.98.54: Be you that true offspring; do not you embrace the misdeed of our father, a deed that was done and that is condemned in the world by the wise.
t.2.98.55: May you, sir, protect Kaikeyī and me and our father, our friends and our kinsmen, all the people of the city and the countryside; may you protect all of this.
t.2.98.56: Where is the forest, and where the duty of a kṣatriya? Where are matted locks, and where the protection of subjects? You ought not to undertake such a self-contradictory course of action.
t.2.98.57: But if you wish to practise only that dharma which is born of hardship, then take on hardship by protecting the four varṇas in accordance with dharma.
t.2.98.58: O knower of dharma, those who know dharma declare that of the four āśramas the householder's life is the best stage; how then can you think to abandon it?
t.2.98.59: Indeed, in learning, in rank, and in birth I am but a child compared to you. How then shall I, such as I am, govern the earth while you remain?
t.2.98.60: I am a mere boy, lacking in intelligence and virtues, and inferior in rank as well; left without you, I cannot bring myself to carry on.
t.2.98.61: O knower of dharma, together with your kinsmen, rule according to your own dharma this whole ancestral kingdom, untroubled and free of thorns.
t.2.98.62: Right here, O knower of dharma, let the officiating priests, together with Vasiṣṭha, skilled in sacred mantras, consecrate you with due mantras along with your kinsmen.
t.2.98.63: Consecrated by us, go to Ayodhyā for its protection, as Vāsava, having swiftly conquered the worlds, goes with the Maruts.
t.2.98.64: Discharging the three debts, thoroughly consuming your enemies, and gratifying your friends with all they desire, you yourself must instruct me here.
t.2.98.65: Today, noble one, let your friends rejoice at your consecration; today let your enemies, stricken with fear, flee to the ten directions.
t.2.98.67: With my head bowed I entreat you: show compassion to me and to all your kinsmen, as Maheśvara does toward all beings.
t.2.98.66: O bull among men, wipe away the reproach that falls on me and on my mother, and today protect our revered father from sin.
t.2.98.68: Or else, if you set all this aside and go from here to the forest after all, then I too shall go with you.
t.2.98.69: Even so, though Bharata, in deep distress, entreated him with his head bowed low, Rāma, the lord of the earth, steadfast and firmly established in his father's word, did not set his mind on returning.
t.2.98.70: Beholding that wondrous steadfastness in Rāghava, the people, though sorrowful, attained joy in equal measure. They were grieved that he would not go to Ayodhyā, yet, beholding his firmness in his vow, they rejoiced.
t.2.98.71: The officiating priests, the leaders of the guilds and companies, and likewise the mothers, dazed and with voices choked by tears, praised Bharata as he spoke thus, and, bowing to Rāma, they all together entreated him.
